learn.intro: In 1492 Christopher Columbus reached the Caribbean. Was he a great explorer or an invader? And what changed after 1492, and for whom? This topic puts Columbus on trial and examines the Columbian Exchange.

sections.title: 1. Columbus on trial

blocks.p: In October 1492 Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached islands in the Caribbean (probably the Bahamas, then Cuba and Hispaniola), believing he was near Asia. He made three more voyages (1493, 1498, 1502).
The islands were home to the Taíno people, with their own societies, farming (including cassava), religion and trade. They were not an empty land.

Columbus's journal, which survives through later copies, shows curiosity about the Taíno but also an intention to take control: he noted they could easily be conquered and made to work. He set up Spanish settlements, took Taíno captives to Spain and began forced labour, later formalised as the encomienda system. With disease and violence, this devastated the Taíno within decades.

Historians can hold two ideas at once: Columbus was a skilled navigator, and his arrival began a violent colonial process. We have no written sources by the Taíno from 1492, so their history survives through archaeology, oral tradition and Spanish accounts. That gap is itself a lesson about whose voices survive.

evidence: Columbus reached the Caribbean in October 1492.

sections.title: 2. The Columbian Exchange

blocks.p: The "Columbian Exchange", a term coined by the historian Alfred Crosby in 1972, describes the huge transfer of plants, animals, people, diseases and ideas between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia after 1492.

ul: From the Americas: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao and chilli peppers, which changed diets across Europe, Africa and Asia.
To the Americas: wheat, sugar, coffee, and animals such as horses, cattle and pigs. Horses reshaped many Plains societies.
Disease: smallpox, measles and influenza, to which Indigenous Americans had no immunity.

blocks.p: Historians estimate that Indigenous populations in parts of the Americas fell by 80–90% within about a century of contact, caused mostly by disease, made worse by violence, forced labour and displacement.

The exchange was not equal. Europe gained new foods and wealth; Indigenous Americans faced catastrophe. That is why "discovery" is contested: for the millions already living in the Americas, 1492 was the start of invasion and disease.

evidence: Indigenous populations fell by an estimated 80–90% in parts of the Americas.

sources.title: Columbus's journal of the first voyage
sources.origin: Columbus's log, known mainly through a summary by the friar Bartolomé de las Casas.
sources.purpose: A record for the Spanish monarchs who funded him.
sources.usefulness: Shows Columbus's intentions and first impressions. It is filtered through a later copyist and written to impress his sponsors.

sources.title: Taíno zemi carving
sources.origin: Made by Taíno people; examples are held in museums such as the British Museum.
sources.purpose: Represented spirits or ancestors in Taíno religion.
sources.usefulness: Direct evidence of Taíno beliefs and craft, from their own hands rather than Spanish writing.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: Christopher Columbus: explorer or invader? Reach a judgement.
questions.asks: Weigh Columbus as a skilled navigator against Columbus as the start of colonisation, and reach a qualified judgement.
steps: Decide, using a qualifier; you can argue he was both.
questions.plan: 2 minutes planning, 9 minutes writing, 1 minute checking.
mistakes: Pure celebration or pure condemnation with no evidence

model.t: Columbus is better described as an invader than simply an explorer, although he was both.
He was a skilled navigator who crossed the Atlantic in 1492, but his own journal noted that the Taíno could easily be conquered and made to work.
This meant his arrival began forced labour and Spanish settlement, which, with disease, devastated the Taíno within decades.
Therefore, from the Taíno perspective especially, "invader" is the more accurate description.
